meeting_header:
Date/Time: 2026-09-18 14:27 UTC | Duration: 58m | Platform: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Elena Torres (Redwood SE); Sara Kim (Pinnacle Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (Platform), Priya Nair (CTO), Jon Park (SRE)
summary: POC scoping focused on unit economics for a retrieval-augmented generation feature: discuss per-token estimates, batching and KV cache strategies, SLO targets, pilot timeline (4 weeks), security requirements. Customer wants concrete cost numbers tied to their traces and a bench run. Agreed next steps: share econ worksheet, customer to share traces, Redwood to propose benchmark script and pilot pricing.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I can see most folks are here. We'll keep this tight — goal is to align on a 4-week pilot and nail down unit econ assumptions.
[00:18] Sara (Head of ML): Thanks, yes — we've been evaluating options, cost is... like top of mind. We run a retrieval flow + LLM that averages ~180 tokens generated per request and about 120 tokens in the prompt.
[00:35] Ravi (SE): Cool, can I clarify: is that the combined prompt+response or just the generation?
[00:40] Sara: That's combined, roughly 300 tokens total per inference. Peak qps is ~45, sustained around 20 during business hours.
[00:48] Tom (Platform): And retention — we need to ensure logs and raw transcript data stay in our VPC for 90 days, plus encryption with KMS.
[00:56] Maya: Understood. For the econ model, we usually break it into token cost, CPU/GPU amortization, and operational overhead. For hosted mode we gave an example of $0.00045/token for a 13B-class quantized model at typical batching; for dedicated it looks different.
[01:14] Priya (CTO): Those numbers vary a lot depending on caching and batching, right? If we can hit a 60% prefix cache hit rate the per-token cost drops dramatically.
[01:22] Ravi: Exactly — with KV cache hits you avoid recomputing a lot of context. In our bench runs we commonly see effective token cost reduction by 30–50% with a decent cache. But it depends on user patterns — repetitiveness of prompts, session lengths.
[01:36] Jon (SRE): Quick infra question: we're leaning towards VPC Private deployment for data control. How different is the pricing/latency there versus Redwood Hosted?
[01:44] Elena (SE): Private has two parts — control plane and the data plane. On-prem/VPC will incur a dedicated capacity fee and then a per-GPU amortized charge. Latency often improves slightly since it's colocated, but throughput scaling is something we size in the reserved capacity. Pricing will be on a reserved monthly basis for Dedicated or an enterprise agreement for on-prem.
[02:03] Sara: For the pilot we only have a $7k monthly upper budget for inference costs — is that realistic for our workload?
[02:11] Maya: If we take your traffic at 20 sustained qps, 300 tokens/request, that's ~1.8M tokens per minute? Actually let me do the math: 20 req/s * 300 tokens = 6k tokens/s, *60 = 360k tokens/min; *60 = 21.6M tokens/hour — oops wait that arithmetic seems off, hang on —
[02:36] Tom: (laughs) that's why we love AEs, right?
[02:39] Maya: Sorry, re-calc: 20 req/s * 300 tokens = 6,000 tokens/s; per hour that's 21.6M tokens. Per day that's ~518M tokens (assuming sustained), which is high. But your actual daily average will be lower because sustained is lower than peak. For pilot sizing we usually ask for 1 week of traces so we can compute realistic monthly estimates.
[02:58] Sara: We'll provide 3 days of traces.
[03:02] Ravi: Great. For ballpark, if we assume hosted per-token cost of $0.00045, then 1M tokens ~= $450. So a $7k budget covers ~15.5M tokens — which is only a fraction of those big sustained numbers. If you leverage batching (increase effective tokens per GPU batch) and a 50% KV cache hit rate, you can get to an equivalent per-effective-token of maybe $0.00025–0.0003. That extends the budget to 23–28M tokens.
[03:35] Priya: Can you explain batching tradeoffs? We worry about latency impact for interactive flows.
[03:42] Ravi: Sure. Batching groups concurrent requests to improve GPU utilization. You can configure max batch latency (how long a request waits for batch), max batch size, and adaptive batching. Typical tradeoff: higher batch sizes reduce unit cost but increase tail latency. For interactive UX we tune to keep p95 under your SLO (e.g., 200–300ms).
[03:59] Tom: What about continuous batching vs fixed windows?
[04:02] Ravi: Continuous or streaming-aware batching tends to be better for reducing latency impact — Redwood's runtime has adaptive batching with priority for low-latency routes. We can reserve a low-latency pool for tens of qps and a cheaper high-throughput pool for background requests.
[04:17] Sara: Our success criteria: p95 generation latency < 300ms, cost under $7k for pilot month, and no PII leaving our VPC.
[04:25] Maya: Perfect, that's concrete. We'll map cost targets to two scenarios: hosted minimal friction and private dedicated (VPC) with reserved capacity. We'll also produce per-route econ: low-latency route vs batch route.
[04:37] Jon: On caching: are you doing prefix vs full-response caching? We have many repeated system prompts and doc chunks; we want to avoid regenerating tokens.
[04:46] Ravi: We support prefix/KV caching — you can cache last-n tokens or fixed segments like document embeddings keys. Hit rates depend on your doc chunking and retrieval strategy. If you can share a sample of retrieval keys frequency, we can estimate hit-rate.
[04:59] Sara: We'll share the retrieval logs.
[05:02] Maya: Bench plan suggestion: 1) baseline run with no cache, 2) run with simulated 40/60/80% cache hit rates, 3) run with batching tuned for low-latency (p95 target) and high-throughput. We'll measure cost per effective response, GPU utilization, and p95/p99 latency.
[05:19] Priya: How long does a bench window need to be?
[05:22] Ravi: For stable numbers, 30–60 minutes per scenario during representative load is fine. For burst behavior and autoscaling tests we do a longer run, maybe 2–4 hours.
[05:31] Tom: We have compliance constraints: SOC2, SSO via SAML, RBAC, audit logs. Can you confirm Redwood supports those in Private?
[05:39] Elena: Yes. Private deployments support SAML SSO, RBAC, KMS integrations, and audit logs shipped to your SIEM. We'll send the security packet after this call.
[05:48] Jon: Any special network considerations for benching in our VPC? We need to allow IP ranges and ensure TLS mutual auth with our gateway.
[05:56] Elena: We'll provide an integration checklist — usually a few firewall rules and a service account with limited permissions.
[06:00] Maya: Back to pricing: for the pilot we can propose a capped pilot fee with a committed token budget and overage tiers. We typically do six figures for dedicated but small pilots can be structured as a time-limited reserved pool.
[06:14] Sara: We'd prefer a predictable cap rather than unexpected overages.
[06:17] Maya: Understood — we can do a $7k capped pilot with clearly defined workload envelope. If we exceed the envelope we'll flag and pause or negotiate.
[06:26] Ravi: Important technical note: quantization and kernel selection. If you're using a 13B-like family quantized to 4-bit we see large reductions in GPU memory and cost, but sometimes a small quality delta. We'll include recommendation profiles in the econ worksheet (e.g., fp16 vs q4_0 vs q4_1).
[06:44] Priya: Can you include expected throughput per GPU for the model family? We run microservices and want to know how many GPUs to reserve for production.
[06:51] Ravi: Sure — rough rules of thumb: a single A10-like card might do ~5–10 low-latency requests/s for 13B at p95 < 300ms depending on batch size; an H100 will be much higher. We'll produce specific bench numbers once we have your token distributions.
[07:05] Maya: Let's capture success criteria again: (1) p95 < 300ms for low-latency route, (2) pilot capped at $7k, (3) KV cache hit rate improvement target of 40% to reach target economics, (4) security checklist satisfied.
[07:18] Sara: Sounds good. On timeline: we want pilot started early October. Can you commit to a bench plan and pilot pricing by end of next week?
[07:26] Maya: Yes — we'll send the econ worksheet and pricing by 2026-09-22.
[07:30] Tom: One more operational nuance: we have a multi-tenant service internally; can we map tokens to customer-id routing? We need per-customer cost attribution.
[07:40] Elena: Redwood Console supports token-level breakdowns per API key/route and you can export cost per route or tag. That should solve per-tenant attribution.
[07:50] Jon: Any pitfalls you've seen where customers burned through pilot budgets?
[07:53] Ravi: Two common ones: misestimated token counts (not counting retrieval-generated tokens) and not enabling KV caching early. We'll help instrument instrumentation to capture accurate token counts.
[08:06] Sara: Ok, we'll work on the traces and retrieval logs.
[08:09] Maya: Recap / next steps: Maya send econ worksheet + batching recommendations; Elena share security packet; Ravi send bench script; Tom provide traces. We'll tentatively aim to start pilot week of 2026-10-04.
[08:23] Priya: Thanks, team. This was helpful.
[08:26] Maya: Great, we'll follow up in email with attachments and a calendar invite for the bench kickoff. Appreciate the time.
[08:31] (meeting ends)
notes: Transcript contains typical ASR artifacts: occasional word swaps (KV cash, V PC), speaker overlap; timestamps approximate. Bench plan includes multi-scenario runs and caching/batching permutations. Pilot budget constraint ($7k) is a hard requirement from customer side.
